articles.headline: County Organization.
articles.text:
There has been so much discussion relative to the new law concerning the organization of counties that it seems best to publish the main points and a synopsis of the whole. Section 1, under "County Boundaries and Organization" reads: "Whenever the voters of any unorganized county in this territory shall be equal to one hundred and fifty or upward, and at least one hundred and fifty thereof shall desire to have said county organized, they may petition the governor, setting forth that they have the requisite number of legal voters to form a county organization, and request him to organize said county, as hereinafter provided.

The second section under this head reads: "Whenever the voters of any unorganized county in this territory shall petition the governor, as provided in the preceding section, and the said governor shall be satisfied that such county has one hundred and fifty legal voters, it shall be the duty of the governor, and he is hereby authorized, to call an election in said unorganized county, and fix one or more places in said county as the polling places therein, and shall fix the time for holding said election; and the governor shall thereupon issue a notice of election, which notice shall be substantially in the following form, to-wit: (then follows a form for election notice, not necessary to publish.)

The third section directs that at this election, all officers shall be elected to hold office until the next general election and until their successors are elected and qualified.

The fourth section provides that at this election the county seat shall be chosen, the place receiving the highest number of votes to be the county seat.

The fifth section requires that when the governor has made out the notice of election, he shall cause it to be delivered to the clerk of the district court of the judicial subdivision to which the unorganized county is attached for judicial purposes, (in our case this is Morton county,) at least fifty days prior to the date set for the election. At least forty days prior to the election, the said clerk shall, with the assistance of the chairman of the board of county commissioners and register of deeds of said county, divide the unorganized county into election precincts, in accordance with the notice, regard being had to the convenience of the voters. The clerk must then publish and circulate the notice of election, together with a further certificate, issued by him.

Section sixth provides that the said clerk, chairman and register of deeds shall, at the same meeting in which the above business is transacted, appoint three capable and discreet persons, possessing the qualifications of electors, to act as judges of election at each polling place in the county.

Section seventh provides that five notices of the election be posted in conspicuous places throughout the county, at least twenty days before the election.

Section eighth provides that in case there should be a vacancy in the office of judge of election, the vacancy shall be filled by the vote of the electors then present at the place of voting. This section also provides that the judges shall choose two persons possessing the qualifications of voters, to act as clerks of such election.

The eighth section provides that the previous laws in reference to elections shall be in force, except those conflicting with the provisions of this act.

The ninth section provides that the governor shall, at least thirty days before the election, appoint a supervisor of election to serve at each polling place in the county. Each supervisor shall make oath that he is neither directly or indirectly interested in the location of any county seat in said county and is not the owner of any land or interests therein.

The tenth section provides that the supervisors shall furnish ballot-boxes and poll-books, failing in which, they may be furnished by any qualified elector.

The eleventh section provides that the supervisor shall use every means in his power to prevent any fraud in the election.

The twelfth section provides that the supervisor can do almost anything he sees fit in his efforts to secure a fair election.

Section thirteen provides for the punishment of anyone who in any way interferes with the officers of election or the sanctity of the ballot.

Section fourteen provides that the ballot be folded by the elector and handed to one of the judges of election and if all or a majority of the judges and supervisors are satisfied that the person offering the vote is a legal voter, the clerks shall enter his name and number in the poll-books and the judges and supervisors shall immediately endorse on the back of the ballot the voter's number and immediately deposit the ticket in the ballot-box.

The fifteenth section provides that no adjournmen shall be taken from the time the first vote is polled until all the votes have been counted and the result publicly announced. The ballots, as counted, shall then be strung on a stout cord and the cord then knotted and the knot sealed. They are then to be enveloped and sealed by the judges in the presence of the supervisor. After this, they are to be replaced in the ballot-box, which is then to be sealed and delivered to the supervisor.

The sixteenth section provides that one of the poll-books shall be enclosed in the ballot-box and the whole deposited with the clerk of the district court having jurisdiction over the newly organized county. The other poll-book is to be deposited in the office of the register of deeds of the county having jurisdiction, to be kept as a public record.

Section seventeen provides that any election officer, who shall be guilty of, or connive at any fraud, shall, upon conviction be punished by a fine not exceeding five thousand dollars and by an imprisonment of from one to five years in the penitentiary.

Section eighteen provides that the register of deeds and a majority of the county commissioners of the senior county, shall canvass the returns and on separate sheets of paper count the votes for officers and the location of the county seat. The register shall then issue certificates of election to the person receiving the highest number of votes for each office and the place receiving the highest number of votes shall be declared the county seat.

Within twenty days after this canvass of votes the officers elected shall qualify. If any fail to qualify within thirty days his office shall be declared vacant and shall be filled according to law.

The concluding sections of the law specify that the commissioners newly elected shall divide the county into commissioners' districts, not to be changed oftener than once in three years. At the ensuing general election one commissioner shall be chosen for one year, one for two years and one for three years. After that, one is to be elected annually.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy prints a section-by-section synopsis of the new territorial law on organizing counties, noting that the unorganized county is attached to Morton county for judicial purposes.

articles.text: Robert Tombs, the "great unreconstructed" died Tuescay night at Washington, Ga.
articles.summary: Death of Robert Toombs at Washington, Georgia.

articles.text: Minneapolis has expended eight million and a half of dollars in building during the last year.
articles.summary: Minneapolis building expenditure for the year.

articles.text: B. Gratz Brown, who ran for vice-president in 1872, on the Greely ticket, died last Saturday in St. Louis.
articles.summary: Death of B. Gratz Brown in St. Louis.

articles.text: The Merrill House at Glendive, burned last Sunday morning. The loss is $41,000, insurance $26,000. E. C. Waters, the proprietor, expects to rebuild in the spring.
articles.summary: The Merrill House hotel at Glendive burned; proprietor E. C. Waters plans to rebuild.

articles.text: Slosson, Shaefer and Vignaux will begin next Monday a series of games to decide the billiard championship of the world. This time the games will be continued until one is victor.
articles.summary: Coming world billiard championship series.

articles.text: A fire in Bismarck Monday, burned out Schonberg's, boot and shoe store, Edick Bros. cigar factory and did about $600 damage to the First Nat. Bank block. The total loss is about $15,000. Insurance about $7,000.
articles.summary: A Bismarck fire burned out Schonberg's boot and shoe store and Edick Bros. cigar factory.

articles.text: A fund is being raised for a monument over the tomb of Thomas A. Hendricks. It would seem that there are enough languishing monument funds in the country now, without adding another to the list.
articles.summary: Packard scoffs at a monument fund for Vice President Hendricks.

articles.text: Senator Harrison introduced into the Senate Tuesday, a bill for the admission of a part of Dakota. Southern Dakota is doing well to have its statehood bill introduced thus early in the session, for it will have a hard row to hoe before it becomes a state.
articles.summary: Senator Harrison introduced a bill to admit southern Dakota as a state.

articles.text:
There seems to be good foundation for the rumor that the American Express Co's. proposition to the Northern Pacific to buy out their express line, will be accepted. To-day's meeting of the N. P. directors in New Yurk will probably decide the matter.

[Since the above was put in type, the American has bought out the Northern Pacific Expr[ess] C[o]. and after the first of January will have exclusive control of the express business on the Northern Pacific.
articles.summary: The American Express Co. bought out the Northern Pacific Express and takes over N. P. express business after January 1.

articles.text: Through freight rates from St. Paul to Black Hills points have been made via the Fremont, Elkhorn & Missouri Valley R. R. They range from $2.30 on fifth class to $3.30 on first class merchandise. This is really no reduction of rates.
articles.summary: New through freight rates from St. Paul to the Black Hills via the Fremont, Elkhorn & Missouri Valley road.

articles.text: Great fear is expressed that there will be another out-break in Canada on account of the death of Riel and his Indian associates. The Indians especially are becoming hostile and it is thought that Gabriel Dumont is planning to head a rebellion.
articles.summary: Fears of a new Canadian uprising after Riel's execution.

articles.text: The state legislature of southern Dakota met at Huron on Monday. Govenor Mellette sent in his message Tuesday and Judges Moody and Edgerton were elected senators. We wonder if anything will finally come of what all in the north think is a gigantic farce.
articles.summary: The southern Dakota state legislature met at Huron, heard Mellette's message and elected Moody and Edgerton senators.

articles.text: Representative Seney of Ohio, will, as soon as possible, introduce a bill in Congress to repeal the civil-service law. There is not one capable business man in a thousand who can pass an examination according to law and it should certainly be amended or repealed. We doubt however, if enough back-bone can be found in Congress to repeal it.
articles.summary: Packard backs repeal of the civil-service law proposed by Rep. Seney.

articles.text: The president has asked that immediate relief be granted to the northern Cheyenne Indians on the Rosebud and Tongue rivers. There are reported to be 700 Indians on these rivers, without food.
articles.summary: The president asked relief for 700 starving northern Cheyennes on the Rosebud and Tongue rivers.

articles.text: The Apaches are giving serious trouble in Arizona. Every day brings new stories of murders, and the troops seem entirely unable to cope with the Indians. It would be a good scheme to raise a company of cow-boys to put down the marauders.
articles.summary: Packard suggests a company of cowboys to fight the Apaches in Arizona.

articles.text: To-day and yesterday have been as beautiful days as any we have had during the fall. We just had a taste of winter, enough to get cattle used to it, when genuine fall weather has again set in. Cattlemen are enthusiastic over the prospect.
articles.summary: Fine fall weather returned after a brief taste of winter, pleasing cattlemen.

articles.text: The Cheyennes and Arapahoes are again dissatisfied. They were anxious to have the cattlemen leave but now that they do not get money for leases they are becoming turbulent. It has been so long since Indians any where have received a good thrashing that it will probably be necessary to give them one soon.
articles.summary: Packard comments harshly on unrest among the Cheyennes and Arapahoes over lost lease money.

articles.text: From late British returns, it is found that for the year ending June 4, 1885, of 682,693 cattle born in England, 134,941 died of disease. In Wales, the number of cattle born was 147,702, of which 18,439 died. The total for Great Britain shows that 1,072,409 cattle were born and that 193,056 died. The above figures from the Drovers' Journal, furnish a fine comment on England's restrictions on our live stock importations. Such a terrible per cent. of loss would seemingly paralyze any stock interest. Such a showing of fatal diseases in England also calls for rigid quarantine measures on the part of our government. Nine-tenths of the disease among cattle in the United States came originally from English cattle and in view of the state of things now prevalent there, too strict measures cannot be adopted against them.
articles.summary: British cattle-disease figures prompt a call for quarantine against English cattle.

articles.summary: Reading notice for the Drug Store's jewelry and plated ware.

articles.text: If you are in need of a good tea-set, either in figured gold or china, H. M. Jorgens can fit you out.
articles.summary: Reading notice: tea-sets at H. M. Jorgens's.

articles.text: The ice-houses are being cleaned out preparatory to the ice season. C. F. Ellison will have charge of the work.
articles.summary: Ice-houses being readied for the ice harvest under C. F. Ellison.

articles.text: The Drug Store is the place to buy anything you want in the way of fancy goods or notions.
articles.summary: Reading notice for fancy goods at the Drug Store.

articles.text: C. F. Ellison has almost completed his cozy dwelling house and it will soon be ready for occupancy. His wife is now in Mandan.
articles.summary: C. F. Ellison's new house is nearly finished; his wife is in Mandan.

articles.text: Christmas is coming, and you can get anything you want in the way of presents of H. M. Jorgens.
articles.summary: Reading notice: Christmas presents at Jorgens's.

articles.text:
The agent at Mingusville has returned and W. H. Minty has resumed his old place here as night operator, that was filled by Dan. Williams during his absence.

[The above was changed to-day by Greene going to Dickinson, Minty becoming day operator and Williams, night operator.
articles.summary: Changes among Medora's railroad telegraph operators: Greene to Dickinson, Minty day operator, Williams night operator.

articles.text: H. M. Jorgens has just opened up a complete stock of crockery and glassware. Now is your time to purchase.
articles.summary: H. M. Jorgens opened a stock of crockery and glassware.

articles.text: Two horses belonging to the SOHO cattle Co. were in Red Cloud's alias George Wood's posession when he was killed by Chris Gross. They will be brought back to the ranch soon.
articles.summary: Two Soho Cattle Co. horses were found with Red Cloud, alias George Wood, when Chris Gross killed him.

articles.text: Alden Eaton returned Monday evening from his eastrn trip. He was visiting in Pittsburgh and Meadville. He reports having a delightful time, but glad to get back to the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: Alden Eaton returned from Pittsburgh and Meadville.

articles.text: Fred Willard's residence will be finished in about two weeks. It will be comfortably arranged, of good size and will present a neat appearance. Copeland & Williamson have the contract.
articles.summary: Fred Willard's residence, built by Copeland & Williamson, is nearly done.

articles.text: Remember that you can buy your fancy goods and notions as cheap at the Drug Store in Medora as you can anywhere this side of St. Paul. Besides this you may draw a prize to exceed the value of the goods.
articles.summary: Reading notice for the Medora Drug Store and its prize drawing.

articles.text: Charlie Eaton returned from Pittsburgh last night. Between the enjoyment of his eastern trip, his pleasure at returning to the Bad Lands and his endeavors to again get used to a cow-boy hat after wearing a dude outfit so long, his sensations are as badly mixed as are the reports concerning the likelihood of there being a new Mrs. Eaton in the spring.
articles.summary: Charlie Eaton returned from Pittsburgh amid rumors of a spring wedding.

articles.text: Win. Roberts and a number of other prisoners in the Miles City jail made an attempt to escape recently. They got through the floor of a cell but then ran across a plate of chilled steel that stopped further progress. The jail officials could not find the tools with which the work was done but a diet of bread and water for four days made Win. weaken and show up a case knife, with which the job was done.
articles.summary: Win. Roberts and other prisoners failed in an escape attempt from the Miles City jail.

articles.text: H. M. Jorgens wishes to announce to the public that he has connected with his business a gift enterprise. Buying three dollars' worth of fancy goods, notions or jewelry entitles you to a number in the gift enterprise. Every number draws a prize varying in price from ten cents to ten dol[la]rs.
articles.summary: Jorgens starts a gift enterprise: every $3 purchase earns a prize number.

articles.text: An extract from the marriage license notices in the Pittsburgh Penny Press, of Dec. 8, sent us by Charlie Eaton, makes rather interesting reading. It states that on that date a marriage license was issued to John B. Walker and Jennie Dolish, of Irwin station, Penn. Hereafter the Cow Boy will pose as a prophet. It will be remembered that in spite of the fact, that Walker was reported to be in Helena, the Cow Boy predicted that he could be found in Pennsylvania.
articles.summary: A marriage license was issued Dec. 8 in Pennsylvania to John B. Walker and Jennie Dolish, as the Cow Boy had predicted.

articles.text:
We refrained from mentioning anything concerning the proposed reduction in the depot force here in our last issue, hoping that the change would not be made in Mr. Maxwell's position. A large remonstrance was sent in by our citizens to the proposed change, and Auditor Sharkey and route-agent Stedman also sent in protests. It seems that the change is to be made, however, and Mr. Maxwell will probably accept a position in the Wells-Fargo company at Helena. He has been altogether the most popular agent we have ever had here and there is no one but that regrets seeing the change made.

[Since the above was put in type, Mr. Maxwell has decided to remain in Medora and will accept the agency of the Wells-Fargo.
articles.summary: Despite citizen protests the depot force is being cut; agent Maxwell will stay in Medora as Wells-Fargo agent.

articles.text: An insurance agent was here last week soliciting trade in a way that showed either him or the company he represented, to be a fraud. He tried to do business on a sliding scale of rates that no responsible insurance company would authorize. He offered to insure a dwelling house with an adjacent exposure for one per cent. This is a fraud on the face of it, as no responsible company offers such a rate. All can easily see that it is to their interest to insure with a home agent, who will certainly look after the policy holders' interests better than a tramp agent of a snide company.
articles.summary: Packard warns against a traveling insurance agent offering suspiciously low rates.
